newsitem.title: USA: Advanced Fibre takes on rival telecoms.
newsitem.headline: Advanced Fibre takes on rival telecoms.

text.p: Less than a year after its initial public offering, fiesty Advanced Fibre Communications Inc. is taking on much larger companies in a high-stakes bid to modernise phone networks.

Based in Petaluma, Calif., Advanced Fibre has convinced phone companies such as Sprint Corp. and several regional Bell operators to use its equipment to ease the burden of heavy voice, data and video traffic travelling on their lines.
The growing number of orders for the system has nearly doubled the company's first-quarter revenues from the year-ago period to more $44 million.
Investor interest has also pushed the stock above $54, nearly twice its initial offering price last October.
"It's a fabulous company," said James Kedersha at Cowen & Co, which helped underwrite the offering. "It's the best IPO in telecommunications equipment in the last five years."

Kedersha and other analysts said Advanced Fibre had an advantage over rivals because its so-called next generation digital loop carrier was more flexible and efficient than similar systems on the market.
"These guys have a leg up in the industry," he said.
How long its lead will last is another matter, however.

The company's chief executive, Don Green, said in an interview that the system allowed phone companies to handle more calls and service a wider area in the local loop that connects the "last mile" of wire between their central offices and customer homes and businesses.
Green said the system, known as the UMC 1000, also supported any combination of transmission cables from copper to fiber optic. Other carriers can only handle copper cable.
"This tool will allow telephone companies to gracefully reduce the amount of traffic that they have on their existing networks," he told Reuters.
In recent months, Advanced Fibre has won supply contracts with regional Bell companies, including the Pacific Bell unit of SBC Communications Corp. and Ameritech Corp.

"We are in a similar situation with BellSouth Corp.," said Green. "They have 20 systems to evaluate (and) we are hoping to get to where we will be discussing a specific contract in the not too distant future."
A spokesman for Advanced Fibre said clients like GTE Corp. and Ameritech were using the system in low-density residential areas such as suburban neighbourhoods.
Advanced Fibre gets about a third of its revenues from foreign clients in Brazil, China, France and elsewhere.
Andy Schopick at Nutmeg Securities saw Advanced Fibre easily meeting earnings forecasts for the second quarter. "(It's) still on track to deliver the best growth," he said.
First Call's analyst consensus sees earnings for the quarter at 18 cents a share, against nine cents in the year-ago period.

Stephen Levy of Salomon Brothers said the stock's high price was partly due to optimism about technology stocks in general. "People are paying a multiple for stocks in general and even more for hyper-growth stocks," he said.
Advanced Fibre traded around $53.50 on Nasdaq on June 4.
"(But) you have to be ready for a rollercoaster ride," said Nutmeg's Schopick, referring to the stock's volatility due to the company's small size. "It ain't for the faint at heart."

Green said the company had already begun shipping the latest version of the UMC 1000 before its official unveiling at the recent Supercomm '97, a telecommunications equipment convention in New Orleans.
"It's in our best interest to get as many of these systems installed as possible," he said, adding that it had sent the new one to about 100 clients, including GTE and Sprint.
The new system has 60 times the transmission capacity of the previous one and can manage up to 2,000 access lines simultaneously, he said.
Nevertheless, competition is fierce.
Salomon's Levy said dominant players such as DSC Communications Corp. and Lucent Technologies Inc. were well established in the industry, having developed strong links to telephone companies.
